translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

The August Ming grandly received the Mandate of Heaven and unified the myriad regions. His Majesty, with the [… two illegible characters] of sacred literary accomplishments and divine martial valor, succeeded to the great dynastic heritage and renewed civil rule. In the [… three illegible characters] of the Xuande reign era, upon the scheduled time for evaluating the outstanding and promoting the worthy, the tribute scholars from the commanderies and principalities came [… five illegible characters]. Minister of Rites Your Servant [Hu] Ying 胡濙 and Vice Minister Your Servant [Jiang] Jia 蔣嘉 [… fourteen illegible characters], along with Your Servant Ji 驥, Your Servant Yongqing 永清, Your Servant Heling 鶴齡, Your Servant Ya 雅, Your Servant Zhuan 撰, Your Servant Ci 賜, [… five illegible characters] Shoufu 壽夫 as Associate Examiners, Your Servant Sikuan 思寛 and Your Servant Xian 憲 as Monitoring Examination Officials, together with lesser [… three illegible characters] officials, were all carefully selected for their roles. Your Servant [Jin Youzi 金幼孜 / Wang] Ying 王英 and others received the imperial command and, from dawn to night, reverently and carefully graded and reviewed their essays, obtaining one hundred men who met the standard; indeed, the impartiality of the selection was thereby [… seven illegible characters]. Although the dynasty's advancement and employment of the worthy and talented does not follow a single path, it places the greatest weight on the examination degrees. [… seventeen illegible characters]…

title: 宣德五年會試錄
text:
太祖
太宗
仁宗皇帝聖聖相承至仁大德卓冠千古而
求賢圖治恒若未至士之登第者多顯
擢之俾奮厥庸以昭其聲光
皇上繼承
三聖謨烈之盛
道德之純中正明如日月化理之隆
===
致庶政而尤重於賓興之選蓋欲簡
之也公取之也嚴尤得實才而用之耳
古者縣爵禄以待天下之士故於士也
取之專用之不輕待之彌厚如是者必
冀其有成績而士亦自重罔或自怠逸
必思以盡其才之用相與翊贊洪猷恢
弘功業而垂其聲聞者也今簡士之嚴
待士之厚如此與茲選者將敷對

punctuated: 太祖、太宗、仁宗皇帝聖聖相承，至仁大德，卓冠千古。而求賢圖治，恒若未至。士之登第者，多顯擢之，俾奮厥庸，以昭其聲光。皇上繼承三聖謨烈之盛，道德之純，中正明如日月，化理之隆，致庶政而尤重於賓興之選。蓋欲簡之也公，取之也嚴，尤得實才而用之耳。古者縣爵禄以待天下之士，故於士也，取之專，用之不輕，待之彌厚。如是者，必冀其有成績，而士亦自重，罔或自怠逸，必思以盡其才之用，相與翊贊洪猷，恢弘功業，而垂其聲聞者也。今簡士之嚴、待士之厚如此，與茲選者，將敷對
translation_en:
… Emperors Taizu, Taizong, and Renzong succeeded one another as sage after sage; their supreme benevolence and great virtue stood preeminent through all antiquity. Yet in seeking out worthies and striving for good governance, they ever acted as though they had not done enough. Those scholars who passed the examinations were largely promoted to illustrious offices, enabling them to exert their merits and make bright their renown and glory.

His Majesty has inherited the flourishing counsels and achievements of the Three Sages. In the purity of his moral virtue, he is balanced, upright, and as bright as the sun and moon; in the thriving of his transformative governance, he attends to all the myriad affairs of state, yet places particular weight upon the selection of candidates presented for the examinations. This is because he wishes their screening to be impartial and their selection to be strict, simply so as to obtain men of true talent and employ them.

In antiquity, ranks and emoluments were held out to await the scholars of the world. Therefore, with regard to scholars, their selection was focused, their employment was not undertaken lightly, and their treatment was ever more generous. Acting in this manner, the ruler surely hoped that they would achieve concrete results; and the scholars, for their part, also respected themselves, none daring to indulge in indolence or ease. They surely set their minds on exhausting the usefulness of their talents, joining together to assist in the great plan, expand the achievements of the state, and hand down their renown to posterity. Now, when the strictness in screening scholars and the generosity in treating them are such as this, those who participate in this selection will present their replies…

大廷而致之於用有名爵焉勵其志以建
立事功光昭太平者寧不奮然有為乎
然恒人之情務名而無實勤始而怠終
士則必慎乎此毋或衒名矜能以取一

大廷，而致之於用，有名爵焉。勵其志以建立事功、光昭太平者，寧不奮然有為乎？然恒人之情，務名而無實，勤始而怠終。士則必慎乎此，毋或衒名矜能，以取一時之譽，則庶乎皇上之所以簡拔而用之者，可以無負矣。英忝以進士，備員詞林，仰承聖上明文之治，而擢居禁闈；今乃又叨典文之榮。賢士之進，為邦家之用，敢書此以序茲錄，而為諸士子之勸。

奉議大夫右春坊大學士兼翰林院侍講學士王英謹序。
translation_en:
… the Great Court, and be put to practical use, receiving titles and ranks. In steeling their resolve to establish meritorious deeds and brilliantly manifest the Great Peace, how could they not rouse themselves to vigorous action? Yet it is the way of ordinary men to pursue reputation without substance, and to be diligent at the beginning only to grow lax at the end. Scholars must be vigilant against this: let none peddle their reputation or boast of their abilities merely to win fleeting praise; then perhaps they will not fail to live up to the reason His Majesty has selected and employed them. I, Wang Ying 王英, as a metropolitan graduate (jinshi), have the undeserved honor of filling a post in the Hanlin Academy. Looking up to receive His Sacred Majesty's enlightened and cultured governance, I was promoted to serve in the Forbidden Precincts; and now I have once again been undeservedly favored with the honor of presiding over the literary examinations. As worthy scholars advance to be of service to the state, I venture to write this as a preface to this record and as an encouragement to the candidates.

Respectfully prefaced by Wang Ying, Grand Master for Proper Consultation, Grand Academician of the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, concurrently Expositor-in-waiting in the Hanlin Academy.

四書

朝廷便便言唯謹爾
立則見其參於前也在輿則見其倚於衡也夫
然後行
洋洋乎發育萬物峻極于天優優大哉禮儀三
百威儀三千待其人而後行
易
天之神道而四時不忒聖人以神道設教而
===
天下服矣
上九鼎玉鉉大吉无不利象曰玉鉉在上剛柔
節也
是故法象莫大乎天地變通莫大乎四時縣象
著明莫大乎日月崇高莫大乎富貴
離也者明也萬物皆相見南方之卦也聖人南
面而聽天下嚮明而治蓋取諸此也

立，則見其參於前也；在輿，則見其倚於衡也；夫然後行。
洋洋乎！發育萬物，峻極于天。優優大哉！禮儀三百，威儀三千，待其人而後行。
易
天之神道，而四時不忒；聖人以神道設教，而天下服矣。
上九，鼎玉鉉，大吉，无不利。象曰：玉鉉在上，剛柔節也。
是故法象莫大乎天地，變通莫大乎四時，縣象著明莫大乎日月，崇高莫大乎富貴。
離也者，明也，萬物皆相見，南方之卦也。聖人南面而聽天下，嚮明而治，蓋取諸此也。

Elevating the Four Correlates (Sipei) to share in the offerings, advancing the Ten Savants (Shizhe) to be arranged in sequence, adding enfeoffment titles to the Former Sage, honoring the various masters with noble titles and fiefs, and arraying the worthies in the correlated sacrifices—who were the ones who petitioned to [establish?] these, and how many were there who carried them out? Of the various masters, formerly [there were only?] seventy-two [?]; on what basis did later [rulers/scholars?] increase their number? Among the worthies in the correlated sacrifices, our dynasty dismissed Yang Xiong 楊雄 and advanced Dong Zhongshu 董仲舒, which truly accords with the impartial judgment of ten thousand generations. …be analyzed and set forth in detail? "Vigilance in solitude" (shendu) appears in both books, yet the Great Learning (Daxue) precedes it with the investigation of things and the extension of knowledge, whereas the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) begins with preserving and nourishing. Why is it that the term is the same while the effort differs, and can we hear the purport of this? The learning of Mencius (Mengzi) was obtained from Zisi; commentators say that the words of his Seven Chapters complement these two books as outer and inner—wherein does this truly lie? Are his discussions of the mind and of human nature the same as or different from the words [?] of those two masters? The Way of the sages and worthies is what you ought to study; expound upon it in detail.

Question: Schools are the places for transforming the people and perfecting customs, and take first priority in kingly governance. During the flourishing era of the Three Dynasties, there were schools everywhere both at the capital and in the provinces. In the provinces, district grandees (xiang dafu) of virtuous conduct who had retired from office [?] taught them; why was it that in the capital the Director of Music (siyue) took charge of the regulations of the Grand Academy (Chengjun), and the Music Masters (yueshi) [managed the?] administration of the state schools? Thus the duties of schools in the flourishing Zhou were assigned to the officials in charge of music [?]—what was the intention behind this? And by what Way did they conduct their teaching? When the Han arose, it was not yet far removed from antiquity, and the Erudite Disciples (boshi dizi) received instruction under the Chamberlain for Ceremonials (taichang), which still preserved the lingering intention of antiquity. In the middle period of the dynasty, school officials were established, and the duties of Confucian teachers were first separated out—when was this first instituted? Was their teaching truly different from that of the flourishing Zhou or not? The school system of the Tang was even more detailed, having the distinction between the Two Colleges and the Six Schools; the school administration of the Song was still more thorough, having the division into the Three Halls and the Five Regulations [?]. As for the intentions behind their establishment, the numbers of their students, and the curricula of their instruction and study, can we hear the details of all these? In the Han, the Tang, and the Song, throughout the ages, those who occupied the posts of Confucian teachers had effective methods of education and proper standards as models, sufficient to invigorate the Way of the teacher and bring talent to completion; and those who were students possessed rich classical learning and admirable administrative ability, going forth into office to hone their integrity and reputation and to manifest meritorious achievements, brightly recorded in the historical annals…

Question: Throughout the dynasties, the avenues for selecting scholars have not been uniform, and commentators regard the Han and Tang as the most flourishing. Let us speak of them by citing their general outlines: figures such as Dong Zhongshu 董仲舒, Gongsun Hong 公孫弘, Wei Xiang 魏相, Lu Wenshu 路温舒, Wang Ji 王吉, Gai Kuanrao 蓋寛饒, Ni Kuan 兒寛, and Gong Yu 貢禹 in the Han—some responded to policy questions as Men of Wisdom and Virtue (xianliang), some were recommended as Filial and Incorrupt (xiaolian), some advanced through Classicist (mingjing) examinations, and some through answering policy questions by lot (shece); and figures such as Lou Shide 婁師德, Pei Du 裴度, Han Yu 韓愈, Liu Zongyuan 柳宗元, Li Fengji 李逢吉, Li Jiang 李絳, Lu Zhi 陸贄, Zhang Jiuling 張九齡, Han Xiu 韓休, Jiang Gongfu 姜公輔, and Yuan Zhen 元稹 in the Tang—some passed the metropolitan graduate (jinshi) examination, some advanced through special imperial examinations (zhiju), and some as Men of Wisdom and Virtue (xianliang). Can you point them out one by one? Can you fully recount the realities of their literary learning, personal conduct, and administrative achievements? Yet their worthiness varied, and among them were also those who drew ridicule in their own time and left behind censure for later generations—can those individuals be pointed out and clearly named? In the employment of scholars, what is valued is that they possess moral conduct and righteousness; otherwise, they merely invite the ridicule of noble men and have nothing worth commending. This is what scholars ought to clearly discern; please set it forth in detail.

Comment by Examiner Academician Reader-in-Waiting (shidu) Qian 錢: The essays on this topic throughout the examination hall are stale and tiresome; this one alone is somewhat superior. Only when the effort devoted to words and conduct is at no time [neglected?], is there nowhere that their application will not succeed. For loyalty and trustworthiness, earnestness and respectfulness, are the natural principles of [words and conduct?]. [If one] can preserve these principles in the mind, keeping them constantly before one's eyes without forgetting them, then wherever they are applied, how could they fail to succeed? Such was the meaning of the Master's reply to Zizhang's 子張 question about getting on everywhere.

Now, words are the outward manifestation of conduct, and conduct is the substance of words; words and conduct are the hinge and trigger of the gentleman. How can words be spoken recklessly? One must consider how they will end, making loyalty and trustworthiness their master so that one's words have substance. How can conduct be carried out recklessly? One must examine where it might falter, taking earnestness and respectfulness as its foundation so that one's conduct has constancy. As for these principles, one constantly [retains?] them in one's mind as though they took form before one's eyes. When standing, one sees them standing before oneself—fixing one's thoughts on them here, without a moment's forgetfulness; when in a carriage, one sees them leaning against the crossbar—letting one's thoughts rest on them here, without an instant's separation. Thus one is able to fully realize the principles of one's own mind. Once the principles of one's own mind are fully realized, since all people share this same mind, how could there be any barrier between near and far? Therefore, although the languages of the Eastern Yi 東夷 and Western [Rong 戎?] are mutually unintelligible, yet when one speaks, none will fail to trust…

考試官錢侍講批：場中諸作於此題多用饒氏之言，先後不倫，無可人意。惟此篇敷繹詳明，允為作者，宜在選列。

translation_en:
…how much more so in the nearness of prefectures and districts? Although the customs of the southern Man and northern Di tribes differ, when one acts, there is nothing with which they are not satisfied—how much more so in the closeness of one's own neighborhood and village? I have often observed this in the Book of Changes (Yi), which says: "Words issue from one's person and affect the people; actions issue from what is near and become visible afar." It also says: "Words and actions are the means by which the gentleman moves heaven and earth—must one not be cautious?" Pushing this to its ultimate extent, even something as vast as heaven and earth can be moved by it, how much more so human beings? The Master's words were most earnest and thorough in teaching people. As for a person of fine native substance, once he clarifies this completely, the dregs are wholly transformed and he becomes one body with heaven and earth. In teaching people, where does the sage not employ the ultimate standard? Among the disciples of the sage, Zizhang 子張 pursued externalities and aimed high without being grounded in reality; looking at his question about "attainment" (da), it carried the same intent as his question about "getting through" (xing). When the Master instructed him with these words, Zizhang wrote them upon his sash, from which we can see that in his later years his advancement in learning also reached solid and practical ground.

"How vast! It nourishes all things and rises up to the height of heaven. How abundant and great! The three hundred rules of ceremony and the three thousand rules of demeanor await the proper person before they can be put into practice." [Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong)]
By Chen Zhao 陳詔

Associate Examiner Vice Director Wei 魏 comments: Among the candidates in the examination hall writing on this topic, most resorted to derivative imitation, and on the section "await the proper person before they can be put into practice," none offered any original elucidation. This essay alone analyzes it exhaustively and synthesizes the meaning with precision; it ought to be singled out for distinction.
Examiner Expositor-in-waiting Qian 錢 comments: Most of the essays in the hall on this topic made use of Master Rao's 饒氏 words, resulting in a confused sequence that failed to satisfy. Only this essay elaborates the meaning clearly and thoroughly; he is truly a capable writer and deserves to be placed among the selected.
Examiner Academician Wang 王 comments: On how the Way awaits the proper person to be put into practice, this essay not only elucidates the meaning well, its phrasing is also free of vagueness. His other compositions are likewise superior; how could he be unworthy of passing?

translation_en:
Only because the Way of the Sages reaches the ultimate extreme in both the great and the small does its practice necessarily depend upon human beings. For the Way must obtain the right person before it can be practiced; if there is not the right person, the Way will not be practiced in vain. Once one understands this, one can grasp the purport of the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong).

Moreover, how indeed is the greatness of the Way of the Sages made manifest? Flying, submerging, moving, and rooted beings—these are what make things things; yet that by which they are generated and nourished is nothing other than the single vital energy (qi) of yin and yang and the Five Phases. The circulation of this vital energy is none other than the circulation of this principle, [and thus] the functional efficacy of the Way is able to nurture the myriad things. All-encompassing and universally covering—this is what makes Heaven Heaven; yet that which is undivided and vast is nothing more than the single vital energy of yin and yang and the Five Phases. The pervasion of this vital energy is none other than the pervasion of this principle, and thus the substance and scale of the Way rises to the ultimate height of Heaven. The expression "overflowing" (yangyang) conveys the meaning of flowing movement and full abundance. How the Way reaches the utmost greatness with nothing outside it is already like [this].

Suppose the Way of the Sages had an excess of breadth and greatness yet an insufficiency of fullness and solidity; that too would not be what makes it great. Therefore, as for the three hundred [rules of] ceremonial ritual—such as court audiences, general assemblies, capping, marriage, mourning, and sacrifice—these are all the regulated refinements of Heavenly principle, and this Way resides [in them without] a single instance in which it is absent. As for the three thousand rules of dignified demeanor—such as turning around, advancing and retreating, ascending and descending, and bowing and yielding—these too are all the ceremonial standards of human [affairs], and this Way encompasses them without a single instance in which it is not complete. The expression "abundant" (youyou) conveys the meaning of sufficiency with plenty to spare. How the Way enters into the utmost smallness with no gap in between is in turn like this.

Only then do we know that while "greater virtue makes transformative growth thick and deep" is indeed what makes the Way great, "lesser virtues flow like river currents" is also what makes it great; and while "encompassing Heaven and Earth" is indeed what makes the Way great, "bringing the myriad things to completion in every detail" is also what makes it great. To the greatness of the Way of the Sages nothing indeed can be added; yet how could one distance oneself from human beings in order to practice the Way? Only when one is able to honor the moral nature and carry the greatness of the substance of the Way to its ultimate extreme—then, as for its nurturing the myriad things and rising to the ultimate height of Heaven, even though the Way is so great as to have nothing outside it, we have the means to regulate, complete, assist, and further it, thereby fulfilling our responsibility of participating in the transformative and nourishing processes of Heaven and Earth. And when one follows the path of inquiry and learning and carries the minuteness of the substance of the Way to its ultimate extreme—then, as for ceremonial ritual and dignified demeanor, even though the Way is so small as to have nothing inside it, we have the means to grade, regulate, guard, and model it, thereby fulfilling the work of instituting [and establishing ritual] [?]. Therefore it is said: "It waits for the right person and only then is it practiced." Is this not truly…

…indeed! Furthermore, let us discuss it: what the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) [calls] the Way is in every case what is meant by following one's nature; it is what all under heaven, past and present, follow in common. Why then is it uniquely called the Way of the Sage? Although the Way is followed in common by all people, ordinary people know it without reaching its utmost, and worthies practice it without exhausting it completely. Only the sage knows it to the utmost and practices it completely, embodying in his own person the greatness of this Way. Thus the Way resides in the sage, and therefore it is specially singled out and attributed to him. Yet human nature is the same in the sage as in other men; if scholars [wish to] seek to attain to the level of the sage, they must engage in honoring the moral nature and pursuing inquiry and study before they can succeed.

punctuated: 爲夏也。然懸象□□莫大乎日月，大明當天，容光必照，是即離德之明也。《說卦》聖人於此，不曰「離也者，麗也」，而曰「明也」，盖以麗為附麗之義，而明則物得所麗而明也。向也萬物之出乎震者，今則莫不咸相見于兹焉；向也萬物之齊乎巽者，今則莫不悉覩于此焉。是以洪纖高下有萬之不齊，無不會此亨嘉之美，所謂「品物咸亨」者，斯可見矣；飛潛動植有萬之不一，無不覩此明盛之時，所謂「品物咸章」者，又可知矣。然其所以皆相見乎離者，盖必際夫陽明炎夏之時，則離德之明，宜其當位乎南方之卦也。然離之德為明，而明也□人君出治□□；離之位乎南，而南面者乃人君聽治□□。是以聖人南面而聽天下，恭已無為而聰無不聞，元首惟明而明無不察。文命聲教之誕敷，典章文物之昭著，海宇雖廣，咸囿於麗正之中；生齒雖繁，而皆被其文明之化矣。是果何為而然哉？盖取諸離明之德而致治者也。抑嘗考之《繫辭》，又曰：「黄帝、堯、舜垂衣裳而天下治，盖取諸乾、坤」；「結繩而治，易之以書契，盖取諸夬」者，何歟？然乾、坤變化而無為，故端拱無為之治，非嚮明之君莫能致；夬政明决之意，非體明之德莫能行。然彼各以制器尚象言，此以體卦之德言，合而觀之，益以見體易聖人御南面之正，具離德之盛也。

…is summer. Yet among suspended images that manifest brilliance [?], none are greater than the sun and the moon; when great brightness stands in the center of the sky, wherever light can enter it inevitably illuminates—this is none other than the brightness of the virtue of Li (離). In the Discussion of the Trigrams (Shuogua 說卦), the Sage here does not say "Li means to adhere (li 麗)," but rather says "it means brightness." This is because "to adhere" has the meaning of attachment, whereas "brightness" means that things obtain that to which they adhere and thereby become bright. Previously, the myriad things that emerged in Zhen (震) now all without exception become visible to one another here; previously, the myriad things that were ordered in Xun (巽) now all without exception are beheld here. Therefore, though great and small, high and low, have ten thousand inequalities, none fail to meet in this beauty of flourishing excellence—what is called "the various things all flourishing" can thus be seen! Though flying and submerged creatures, animals and plants, have ten thousand differences, none fail to behold this time of bright abundance—what is called "the various things all brilliantly displayed" can furthermore be known! Yet the reason they all become visible to one another in Li is that they must encounter the time of yang brightness and blazing summer; thus the brightness of the virtue of Li appropriately makes it the trigram positioned in the south.

Now, the virtue of Li is brightness, and brightness is the root [?] by which the ruler issues governance; the position of Li is in the south, and facing south is the position [?] from which the ruler listens to governance. Therefore, the sage faces south and listens to the affairs of All under Heaven: reverently composing himself in non-action, his hearing misses nothing; as the supreme head he is bright, and his brightness leaves nothing unexamined. With the wide promulgation of civil mandates and moral teachings, and the clear manifestation of institutions and cultural objects, although the realm within the seas is vast, all are encompassed within its adherence to correctness; although the populace is numerous, all receive its civilizing and bright transformation. Why indeed is this so? It is because he draws upon the bright virtue of Li to bring about governance.

Yet if we examine the Appended Remarks (Xici 繫辭), why does it also say: "Huangdi, Yao, and Shun let their upper and lower garments hang down and All under Heaven was governed, which they drew from Qian (乾) and Kun (坤)," and "in place of governance by knotted cords, they substituted written documents and tallies, which they drew from Guai (夬)"? Indeed, Qian and Kun transform without deliberate action, so the governance of standing with folded hands in non-action cannot be achieved except by a ruler who faces the light; and the meaning of bright decisiveness in the governance of Guai cannot be carried out except by one who embodies the virtue of brightness. Moreover, those passages each speak in terms of fashioning implements and prizing images, whereas this passage speaks in terms of embodying the virtue of the trigram. Viewing them together, we see all the more how the sage who embodies the Changes (Yi 易) occupies the correct position of facing south and possesses the fullness of the virtue of Li. …

東西南北相距五千里也。謂之「弼成」者，疆理宇内，乃人君之事，非人臣之所得專也。然疆理定矣，使治之之無其方，又豈聖人經國之制哉？故必因其内外之勢，設官以統治焉。是故九州之内，其地皆以封建侯伯矣；今則每州立十二諸侯以為之師，使之相牧以糾群后也。蓋治内不可不詳，故詳其官者，治之以必治也。九州之外，迫於四海，或不以封，而嘗建官治之矣；今則每方各建五人以為之長，而統率之也。蓋治外不可不略，故略其官者，治之以不治也。因其遠近之域，制為繁簡之宜，内外之相承，體統之不紊，經國之制，莫善於此矣。是内而侯牧，外而蕃夷，莫不各脩其職而蹈行於德教，□忘其勞而克成於功績焉。然則因地以疆理而遠近之制同，建官以致治而内外之效一，此大禹輔君之功所以為不可及也歟！或謂舜嘗稱禹「不矜不伐」矣，至此禹乃自序其功，何也？吁！大禹此言，蓋述其治水之本末，而成功之不易，欲君臣上下相與保其治於無窮耳。史臣所謂「文命敷于四海，祗承于帝」者，其以此夫！

…so the distance from east to west and from south to north is five thousand li. The reason he says "assisted in completing" is that demarcating and ordering the realm is the business of the sovereign, not something a subject may arrogate to himself. Yet once the territorial divisions have been fixed, if there were no proper method for governing them, how could that be the sages' system for ordering the state? Therefore, one must establish offices to govern them all in accordance with the relative positions of the inner and outer domains. Thus, within the Nine Provinces, the lands had all been parcelled out as fiefs to marquises and earls; now in each province twelve feudal lords were appointed as leaders to act as pastors and oversee the various rulers. For governing the interior cannot but be detailed; making its offices detailed is to govern them by ensuring thorough governance. Outside the Nine Provinces, pressing close upon the Four Seas, the lands were perhaps not enfeoffed, though officials had previously been established to govern them; now in each direction five men were appointed as chiefs to lead and command them. For governing the exterior cannot but be summary; making its offices summary is to govern them through non-interference. By instituting what is appropriately elaborate or simple according to the nearness or remoteness of the regions, with inner and outer supporting one another and the hierarchical system unconfounded, no institution for ordering the state could be better than this. Consequently, the feudal lords and pastors within, and the tributary peoples and barbarians without, all without exception cultivated their duties and walked in the path of moral instruction, [?] forgetting their toil and able to bring their meritorious achievements to completion. This being so, demarcating the land according to the terrain so that the system was uniform far and near, and establishing offices to achieve good order so that the results were one within and without—is this not why Great Yu's merit in assisting his sovereign is unattainable! Someone might ask: Shun once praised Yu for "not boasting and not bragging"; why then does Yu here recount his own achievements? Alas! In speaking thus, Great Yu was simply recounting the whole course of his regulation of the waters and showing that success was not easily won, desiring that sovereign and ministers, superiors and inferiors, should together preserve this good order without end. When the historian said, "His cultural mandate spread throughout the Four Seas, and he reverently answered to the Emperor," was it not because of this!

… and undivided, without the slightest slackening in the upright Way; when entrusted with official duties and consulted on their plans and counsels, they too are all reverent and careful, fully exhausting their respect and caution without neglecting even the smallest detail. From what indeed does this arise? It may simply be said: in former times King Wen exerted himself in this pure and undivided virtue and carried the work of inspiring and rousing men to the utmost; therefore today the stately multitude of officers and the genial men of goodness are all born within the state of the Sage. Alas! Were it not that King Wen's sagely virtue was grand and flourishing, and that his blessings and bounty were handed down generously to later generations, how could it be like this? In composing this ode, the Duke of Zhou recounted the virtue of King Wen to make clear that the reason the House of Zhou received the Mandate and replaced Shang derived entirely from this, offering it as an admonition to King成 (King Cheng). The first stanza speaks of King Wen's manifest virtue and receipt of the Mandate; the second stanza speaks of his fine reputation handed down through the generations; the third stanza speaks of the abundance of worthy officers obtained; the fourth stanza speaks of the purity of his reverent demeanor; from the fifth stanza onward, it repeatedly dwells upon the mutual responsiveness of Heaven and man and the rise and fall of Yin and Zhou—thus what he used to admonish him was exhaustive indeed. Thereafter, King Cheng truly became an admirable sovereign who preserved the accomplishments of the Zhou, worthy of King Wen; was this not through the power of the Duke of Zhou's instruction and admonition?

Now, that which initiates the beginning of things from above is Qian (Heaven); that which gives birth to things below is Kun (Earth). 求乎是理焉耳理之所在天之所在也天之所在聖
人之所法也夫天之為道四時行而五氣宣藹然陽
和之舒者春夏以燠而生物肅然霜露之慘者秋冬
以寒而成物生者自生莫為其所始成者自成莫為
其所終一出乎自然而無所私焉此天之至公也聖
人既以代天理物為己任則凡九州之內四海之外
無一物而非吾之所當愛無一民而非吾之所當恤
吾於政教之施安能容一毫私意於其間哉亦惟法
天之公而已耳是故於人之善者而加之爵賞不善
者而加之刑罰爵賞以慶之而人知所勸刑罰以威
===
之而人知所懲是則聖人之至公即天之至公也是
之謂法天然天與聖人於至公之中皆有至仁者存
焉霜露所以悴物也而其悴之實所以生之何也往
者過則來者續也刑罰所以威衆也而其威之實所
以愛之何也惡者去而善者遂也論至於是則知聖
人不獨法天之至公抑且同天之至仁矣易言聖人
體天之神道而設教書言惟天聰明惟聖時憲易與
書孔子所贊述者也至漢董仲舒言於武帝則有法
天立道之說仲舒其孔子之徒歟使當時武帝能盡
用之則漢之治不止於漢而已今也

As mild and genial yang warmth unfolds, spring and summer bring warmth and generate things; as stern and severe frost and dew chill, autumn and winter bring cold and bring things to completion. What is generated generates of itself, with nothing artificially initiating its beginning; what is completed completes of itself, with nothing artificially contriving its end. Everything issues from natural spontaneity without any partiality—this is the supreme impartiality of Heaven. Since the sage takes governing things on Heaven's behalf as his own responsibility, then within the Nine Provinces and beyond the Four Seas there is not a single thing that he ought not love, nor a single person among the people whom he ought not show compassion. In dispensing governance and moral instruction, how could he allow a hair's breadth of selfish intent to enter therein? He simply models himself upon Heaven's impartiality, and nothing more. Therefore, upon those among men who are good he bestows ranks and rewards, and upon those who are not good he inflicts punishments and penalties. By celebrating them with ranks and rewards, people know how to be encouraged; by awing them with punishments and penalties, people know how to be deterred. Thus the supreme impartiality of the sage is none other than the supreme impartiality of Heaven; this is what is meant by modeling oneself upon Heaven. Yet within their supreme impartiality, both Heaven and the sage possess supreme benevolence. Frost and dew are the means by which things are withered, yet withering them is in fact the means of giving them life. Why is this? When that which is past moves on, that which is to come continues. Punishments and penalties are the means by which the multitude are awed, yet awing them is in fact the means of loving them. Why is this? When the wicked are removed, the good may flourish. When the discussion reaches this point, one knows that the sage not only models himself upon Heaven's supreme impartiality, but also shares in Heaven's supreme benevolence. The Book of Changes (Yi) says that the sage embodies the marvelous Way of Heaven to establish his teachings; the Book of Documents (Shu) says that Heaven alone is all-intelligent and all-discerning, and the sage takes it as his pattern. 立之行，實萬世學者之所法。盖載此道者，書也；推書以致於行者，人也。苟徒誦習於書，而不以力於行，則於古昔孝子仁人之善行，何以能企及哉？洪惟太祖高皇帝《大誥》首編《諭官生身之恩》暨《諭官無作非為》，所以教導當時臣子之勉於為孝為仁者至矣，誠萬世臣民之所當服膺勿失者也。迨太宗文皇帝推廣前聖之心，復作《孝順事實》、《為善陰隲》二書，所以使天下臣子求古孝子仁人之實行者備矣，誠萬世臣民之所當景仰而效之者。今承明問，謂師其行誼，當以何人為先？愚也何足以言之！雖然，嘗聞之矣：「取法於上，僅得其中；取法於中，斯其下矣。」古之孝子莫過於舜，然舜未易為也，學者先學乎曽參、閔損，斯可矣；古之忠臣莫過於周公，然周公未易至也，學者先學乎韓琦、范仲淹，斯可矣。《書》曰：「知之非艱，行之惟艱。」鯫生小子，未敢自謂能力於行，惟進而教之，幸甚。

translation_en:
… established is truly what scholars for ten thousand generations take as their model. For what carries this Way is books; what extends books so as to carry them into practice is people. If one merely recites and studies books without exerting oneself in practice, then how can one hope to match the good deeds of the filial sons and humane men of antiquity?

I reflect with awe upon how the Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu), in the opening chapters of the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao), "Admonishing Officials on the Grace of Those Who Gave Them Life" and "Admonishing Officials Not to Commit Wrongdoing," instructed the ministers and sons of the time to strive for filial piety and humanity to the utmost degree; this is truly what ministers and commoners for ten thousand generations ought to clasp to their bosoms and never lose. Coming down to the Grand Ancestor, Emperor Wen (Taizong), he broadened and extended the mind of the Former Sage and further composed the two books Biographical Accounts of Filial Piety (Xiaoshun shishi) and Secret Rewards for Doing Good (Weishan yinzhi), whereby he fully enabled the ministers and sons of the realm to seek out the practical conduct of the filial sons and humane men of antiquity; these are truly what ministers and commoners for ten thousand generations ought to look up to and emulate.

Now, having received Your enlightened question asking whom one ought to put first in taking their conduct and righteousness as a model—how am I, in my ignorance, worthy of speaking of this! Even so, I have heard it said: "If one takes the highest as one's model, one barely attains the middle; if one takes the middle as one's model, one ends up with the lowest." Among the filial sons of antiquity, none surpassed Shun; yet Shun is not easy to emulate, so if scholars first learn from Zeng Can 曾參 and Min Sun 閔損, that will suffice. Among the loyal ministers of antiquity, none surpassed the Duke of Zhou; yet the Duke of Zhou is not easy to reach, so if scholars first learn from Han Qi 韓琦 and Fan Zhongyan 范仲淹, that will suffice. The Book of Documents (Shu) says: "To know is not difficult; to act is what is difficult." A petty, shallow youth, I dare not claim to be able to exert myself in practice; I only pray that I may be brought forward and instructed, which would be the greatest fortune.

Among the merits and virtues that extend over ten thousand generations, none is more flourishing than the sageliness of the Master [Confucius]; and the sacrificial rites practiced over ten thousand generations can be examined in the canons of former dynasties. Indeed, since the Master possessed flourishing virtue and great merit, it is fitting that the rites of successive dynasties have been ever augmented and ever more exalted. Thus, whether those subsequently admitted to associative sacrifice were deserving or not cannot go undiscussed. In former times, the Master, with his Heaven-endowed sageliness, transmitted the way of Yao and Shun as his ancestral model, took King Wen and King Wu as his gleaming standards, pared down the Book of Odes (Shijing) and the Book of Documents (Shujing), fixed the rites and music, wrote commentaries on the Changes of Zhou (Zhouyi), and composed the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu). Ten thousand generations look up to his virtue and follow his teachings; this is why from antiquity to the present, from the imperial capital at the top down to the commanderies and districts below, universal sacrifices are offered to him everywhere. Yet although sacrificial rites were practiced at the beginning of the Han, the Shidian (ceremonial libation and offerings to the Former Sage) had not yet been expounded; and although the Shidian was practiced at the beginning of the Tang, its ritual forms were not yet complete. By the Kaiyuan era [713–741], he was given the title of Uncrowned King (Suwang), and his various disciples received the glory of enfeoffed titles of nobility. Each year sacrifices are offered in spring and autumn. The season uses the middle month, taking the middle month as the rectified center of the season, drawing on the balanced equilibrium of yin and yang; the day uses the first ding day, taking ding as belonging to yin fire, drawing on the meaning of cultural brilliance (wenming). The emblems of clouds and thunder are lodged among the lei jars and jue goblets, and odd and even numbers are preserved in the regulations for dou platters and bian baskets. Silk is presented and goblets are advanced, secondary libations are made and offerings are arrayed in order, set forth in vocal songs and performed with musical instruments. Its wine is dark ("mysterious" water/unfermented liquid) and its silk offerings are white—all of these each have their own meaning, serving him with the rites due an Uncrowned King. At the beginning of the Tang, Master Yan [Yan Hui] was made Co-recipient of sacrifices (peixiang), and later on Master Meng [Mencius] was also advanced to this rank. When the Song crossed to the south, Yan [Hui], Zeng [Shen], Zisi [Kong Ji], and Meng [Ke] were first fixed as the Four Correlates (sipei), while Zizhang [Zhuansun Shi] was ranked in sequence among the Ten Wise Ones (shizhe), and ten men such as Kong Li were added to fill out the seventy-two disciples…

… the number of seventy-two. As for the enfeoffment titles of the Former Sage, successive dynasties revered him with ever greater devotion and added ever more posthumous titles. Sometimes he was called Duke Baocheng Xuanni (Exalted Accomplishment and Illustrious Ni), and sometimes Wenxuan Nifu (Cultured and Illustrious Father Ni). In the Tang he was first enfeoffed as King Wenxuan (Cultured and Illustrious King); the Song added the title Zhizheng (Supreme Sage); and Dacheng (Great Perfection) was added by the Yuan. Among those who petitioned to carry these out, in the Zhenguan reign of the Tang there was Fang Xuanling 房玄齡, and in the Kaiyuan reign there was Li Quan 李權. As for increasing the number of those accorded correlate sacrificial rites, from the Tang through the Song and the Yuan, every dynasty had such figures. All the worthies who were admitted to correlate sacrifice were those who upheld the orthodox moral teachings and served as wings to the Six Classics. Yet that Yang Xiong 揚雄, who twisted learning and praised the Xin dynasty, also had his name placed among their ranks. Fortunately, we have encountered an era of sacred enlightenment, which demoted Xiong and promoted Dong Zhongshu 董仲舒—truly in accord with the impartial judgment of ten thousand generations! Yet apart from Xiong, men such as Gongbo Liao 公伯寮, Xun Kuang 荀况, and Wang Bi 王弼 were all contrary to the Way of the Sage and sinned against the orthodox moral teachings; is there not ample ground to deliberate over them? And apart from Zhongshu, in recent times someone like Wu Cheng 吳澂 elucidated the purport of the Six Classics in order to revitalize This Culture; his reputation and conduct indeed ran neck and neck with those of Xu Heng 許衡 in his day. Since Heng is already sacrificed to, Cheng ought also to be promoted. Such is my humble and narrow view; I pray only that Your Excellency forgive my rashness and presumption.

Wu Jie 吳節

When it comes to evaluating the relative merits of teachers and disciples, it is especially pertinent and apt—truly a masterpiece of the policy essay session.

In antiquity, the establishment of schools was the means to perfect men of talent and enrich popular customs; it was the first priority of kingly governance and that whereby the Way of order was brought to completion. Prior to the Three Dynasties, the flourishing of schools could not be surpassed. From the Three Dynasties onward, every ruler of capability and sovereign desiring good order has without exception made this his foremost task—how could scholars fail to discuss it? Since Your Honor has posed this question, I venture to set forth all that I have learned of old in reply.

Indeed, the schools of the Three Dynasties reached complete perfection in the Zhou. In the outer regions, a district (xiang 鄉) of 12,500 families had a district school, presided over by the District Grandee (Xiang dafu 鄉大夫), who promulgated the regulations of instruction to the subdistricts (zhou 州), townships (dang 黨), clans (zu 族), and neighborhoods (lü 閭) so that the people would be taught. In a subdistrict of 2,500 families, the Subdistrict Administrator (Zhouzhang 州長) assembled the people to read the laws and at seasonal intervals practiced archery at the school, honoring merit. In a township of 500 families, the Township Director (Dangzheng 黨正) assembled the people to read the laws and at seasonal intervals practiced the district symposium ceremony at the school, honoring seniority. Even in a neighborhood of twenty-five families there was a village school (shu 塾); retired elders within the neighborhood sat in it morning and evening, and the people going out and coming in invariably received instruction. Such was the administration of the lesser schools (xiaoxue 小學).

In the capital, there was the Greater School (daxue 大學). The Minister of Education (Situ 司徒) exercised overall direction of its affairs, and the Director of Music (Yuezheng 樂正) exalted its instruction. Scholars spent their mornings and evenings within it, immersing themselves at leisure in string music, recitation, singing, and chanting, practicing the deportment of advancing, retreating, bowing, and yielding, having expounded to them the principles of filial piety, fraternal respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness, and enacting for them the regulations of capping, marriage, mourning, and sacrifice, the spring and autumn offerings of vegetables to the former teachers, as well as the rites of the district symposium and the nourishing of the aged. Thus there were means to firm the knitting of their flesh and the binding of their sinews and bones, to regulate their ears and eyes, and to unify their minds and wills. 序教之有其方是以人材衆多禮義興行風俗醇美
此學校之官不可一日廢而先王之治後世不可企
及也漢初去古未遠博士弟子受業太常猶其遺意
後漢明帝以博士之威重者為祭酒司其學政由是
大學太常判而為二為博士者惟知以經義是傳為
生徒者惟知以専門是尚禮樂之器蔵於太常而不
講雖臨雍拜老執經問難果能如周人春夏詩書之
學乎親行射禮果能如周人射御之習乎此原於東
都而其教不古若矣自漢而後天下之言治者曰唐
曰宋唐之學則館有弘文崇文廣文之分學有國學

缺四門書學蓋諸學皆以教公卿之子弟從其父兄
而仕于朝者及庶民之俊秀書律之與筭學則以通
其業者爲之而武學則教之以擊刺騎射以閱其伎
此諸學之所教也唐之三館皆聚皇屬國戚勳臣之
子孫爲生徒而以宰相領之宋之三舍初不限以員名
補外舍生間歲一試補內舍生間歲再試補上舍生
此館舍之所習也是其學校之設既已非先王之舊
而師儒之所以教弟子之所以學又皆忘本而逐末
重外而輕內無復先王之遺意故名雖存而實不□
punctuated: 序，教之有其方。是以人材衆多，禮義興行，風俗醇美。此學校之官不可一日廢，而先王之治後世不可企及也。漢初去古未遠，博士弟子受業太常，猶其遺意。後漢明帝以博士之威重者為祭酒，司其學政，由是大學、太常判而為二。為博士者，惟知以經義是傳；為生徒者，惟知以専門是尚；禮樂之器蔵於太常而不講。雖臨雍拜老，執經問難，果能如周人春夏《詩》、《書》之學乎？親行射禮，果能如周人射御之習乎？此原於東都，而其教不古若矣。自漢而後，天下之言治者曰唐、曰宋。唐之學，則館有弘文、崇文、廣文之分，學有國學、大學、四門、律學、筭□有學之别；宋之學，則增武學而缺四門、書學。盖諸學皆以教公卿之子弟従其父兄而仕于朝者，及庶民之俊秀；書、律之與筭學，則以通其業者為之；而武學則教之以擊刺騎射，以閱其伎：此諸學之所教也。唐之三館，皆聚皇属、國戚、勲臣之子孫為生徒，而以宰相領之；宋之三舍，初不限以員名，補外舍生，間歳一試補内舍生，間歳再試補上舍生：此舘舍之所習也。是其學校之設，既巳非先王之舊，而師儒之所以教，弟子之所以學，又皆忘本而逐末，重外而輕内，無復先王之遺意，故名雖存而實不□
translation_en:
…proper sequence, and their instruction had its proper method. Therefore men of talent were numerous, rites and righteousness flourished, and customs were pure and admirable. This is why the offices of schools could not be dispensed with for even a single day, and why the governance of the former kings could never be equaled by later ages.

At the beginning of the Han dynasty, antiquity was not yet far removed, and the Disciples of the Erudites received instruction under the Chamberlain for Ceremonials (Taichang), which still preserved the lingering intent of antiquity. Emperor Ming of the Later Han appointed the most dignified and respected of the Erudites as Chancellor (Jijiu) to take charge of educational administration; from this point on, the National University (Taixue) and the Chamberlain for Ceremonials were split into two. Those who served as Erudites knew only to transmit the meanings of the Classics, while those who were students knew only to prize specialized expertise; the instruments of rites and music were stored away with the Chamberlain for Ceremonials and were no longer expounded. Even though the emperor visited the Bright Hall (Biyong) to pay homage to the aged and held the Classics to ask difficult questions, could this truly match the Zhou people's study of the Odes and Documents in spring and summer? And even though he personally performed the archery ritual, could this truly match the Zhou people's practice of archery and charioteering? This originated in the Eastern Capital [Luoyang], and its instruction was no longer equal to that of antiquity.

From the Han onward, those in the world who speak of good governance name the Tang and the Song. In the schools of the Tang, the institutes were divided into the Institute for the Advancement of Literature (Hongwen guan), the Institute for the Veneration of Literature (Chongwen guan), and the Institute for the Extension of Literature (Guangwen guan); the schools were differentiated into the School for the Sons of the State (Guoxue), the National University (Taixue), the School of the Four Gates (Simen xue), the School of Law (Lüxue), the School of Mathematics (Suan[xue]), and [Calligraphy] [?] (書學). In the schools of the Song, the Military School (Wuxue) was added, while the School of the Four Gates and the School of Calligraphy (Shuxue) were lacking. In general, the various schools were all used to teach the sons and younger brothers of high officials who followed their fathers and elder brothers in serving at court, as well as the outstanding talents among the common people. The Schools of Calligraphy, Law, and Mathematics were undertaken by those who were proficient in those professions, whereas the Military School taught them fencing, thrusting, horsemanship, and archery so as to review their skills: this is what the various schools taught.

The Three Institutes of the Tang all gathered the descendants of the imperial clan, consort relatives, and meritorious officials as students, and placed a Grand Councilor in charge of them. In the Three Halls system of the Song, initially there was no fixed quota of students when filling the Outer Hall (Waishe); every other year an examination was held to fill the Inner Hall (Neishe), and after another two years a further examination was held to fill the Upper Hall (Shangshe): this is what was practiced in the institutes and halls. Thus the establishment of their schools was already no longer the old system of the former kings, and the means by which teachers and Confucian scholars taught, as well as the means by which disciples studied, all forgot the root to pursue the branches, emphasizing the external while slighting the internal, with nothing left of the lingering intent of the former kings. Therefore, although the name remained, the reality did not…

賀德仁之彬彬文質韓昌黎之遑遑仁義陽城之進
退可則鄭穆之諸生請留是皆卓然以師道自立矣
然其為法也嚴為道也尊言行而身化之胡翼之盖
其尤也為生徒者若李膺之名重一時何蕃之聲振
六館范純仁之直温錢公輔之簡諒皆以豐功偉節
顯于當世傳諸後來矣然求其學極聖人之精微行
合君子之純粹兄弟俱以道學顯於無窮者莫程伊
川若也學校之制師生之詳欲備舉而歷陳之恐留
更僕風簷寸晷姑以比復明問未知是否惟進而教
===
之幸甚

punctuated: 矣。求其屹砥柱於中流，回狂瀾於既到，居師儒者，如賀德仁之彬彬文質，韓昌黎之遑遑仁義，陽城之進退可則，鄭穆之諸生請留，是皆卓然以師道自立矣；然其為法也嚴，為道也尊，言行而身化之，胡翼之盖其尤也。為生徒者，若李膺之名重一時，何蕃之聲振六館，范純仁之直温，錢公輔之簡諒，皆以豐功偉節顯于當世，傳諸後來矣；然求其學極聖人之精微，行合君子之純粹，兄弟俱以道學顯於無窮者，莫程伊川若也。學校之制、師生之詳，欲備舉而歷陳之，恐留更僕。風簷寸晷，姑以比復明問，未知是否，惟進而教之，幸甚。
translation_en:
… Indeed, if one seeks those who stood firm like the Pillar Rock in midstream and turned back the raging waves after they had already broken—among those who occupied the position of Confucian teacher, such men as He Deren 賀德仁, with his harmonious balance of refinement and substance; Han Changli 韓昌黎 (Han Yu 韓愈), ever urgent in his pursuit of benevolence and righteousness; Yang Cheng 陽城, whose advancing and withdrawing served as a model; and Zheng Mu 鄭穆, whom the students petitioned to retain—all of these stood out preeminently in establishing themselves through the Way of the Teacher. Yet in the strictness of his methods, the venerability of his Way, and his transforming others through personal example as his words were put into practice, Hu Yizhi 胡翼之 (Hu Yuan 胡瑗) was surely the most outstanding among them. Among those who were students, such men as Li Ying 李膺, whose renown carried weight throughout his age; He Fan 何蕃, whose reputation resounded through the Six Halls; Fan Chunren 范純仁, upright yet mild; and Qian Gongfu 錢公輔, concise and trustworthy—all became illustrious in their own time through abundant achievements and noble integrity, handing down their names to posterity. Yet if one seeks someone whose learning plumbed the subtle mysteries of the sages, whose conduct matched the pure flawlessness of the gentleman, and who together with his brother became endlessly illustrious for the Learning of the Way (Daoxue 道學), there was none like Cheng Yichuan 程伊川 (Cheng Yi 程頤).

As for the institutions of schools and the detailed accounts of teachers and students, were I to enumerate them completely and set them forth one by one, I fear it would take so long as to require changing the attendants waiting upon you. Beneath the wind-swept eaves, with only an inch of shadow on the sundial, I provisionally offer this [reading 此 for 比?] in reply to your enlightened question. I do not know whether it is correct; I only pray that you will bring me forward and instruct me, which would be my greatest fortune.

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the spring of the fifth year of the Xuande era [1430], the tribute scholars from across the realm who gathered for examination at the Ministry of Rites numbered two thousand. Ahead of time, Your Servant [Hu] Ying 胡濙, the Minister, and Your Servant [Zhang] Jia 張嘉, the Vice Minister, reported this to the throne. His Majesty commanded Your Servant [Wang] Ying 王英, Your Servant [Qian] Xili 錢習禮, and others to examine them. On the jimao day of the second month [March 3, 1430], we entered the examination compound. All those officiating inside and outside without exception held the imperial command in reverent awe and were diligent in their duties. Selecting those whose essays met the standard, we obtained one hundred men, all representing the finest choices of the age. When the Record of the Metropolitan Examination was completed, the competent authorities had me write a postface at the end.

Now, from of old, when worthy talents are born into the world, they must be of service to the state; when a ruler commissions the worthy, he must make strict the methods of selection and recommendation. Only when the methods of selecting them are strict and the rites for treating them are generous will men of extraordinary talent and uncommon ability who emerge from among them gladly be of service, devoting themselves to official careers in order to assist in bringing about the good governance of the state. Reverently considering our Sacred Dynasty, Heaven opened up the fortune of culture, and the successive Emperors rose in turn, …

translation_en:
… their civil virtue and martial achievements surpass those of antiquity. Moreover, they were all earnestly devoted to seeking out the worthy and promoting good governance, so as to exalt the enterprise of great peace for ten thousand generations. They expanded the schools to nurture outstanding talents and attached great importance to the examination system to raise up the worthy and capable. Because they have long been transformed and guided, and are elevated and employed with ritual propriety, there are none among the scholars within the四 seas who do not seize the moment to rouse themselves, rising up to render service at Court. Those whose meritorious deeds and renowned reputations have made them magnificent and famous ministers of the age, one after another, are beyond count. Oh, how flourishing!

His Majesty, with divine and sage virtue, carries forward the Way of succession and continuation. At the beginning of his reign, he greatly renewed governance and has been particularly circumspect in the selection of metropolitan graduates (jinshi). All you scholars were born in an era when the literary fortune is flourishing, at a time when the dynasty is at the height of its prosperity and worthy talents are employed together. Once you have, through your learning, been recommended in the provinces, advanced by the authorities, and again presented at Court to respond to and extol the auspicious mandate of the Sage Son of Heaven, you cause everyone at court and in the countryside to admire your glory and honor. This is truly an extraordinary encounter for the many scholars, and a grand event of our illustrious age. Soon you will enjoy official emoluments and positions, and serve with distinction both inside and outside the capital; …

…How could they become complacent after having attained success, or slacken in their resolve to exert themselves further, thereby betraying what they have learned? It is expected that they will exhaust their hearts and minds, display their utmost loyalty, attend to their official duties, and spread their renown and glory, causing all people in the realm to praise the flourishing success of the examination system in obtaining capable men. Thus they will fulfill the Court's intention in selecting the worthy and employing the capable, and will also demonstrate the completeness of the scholars' learning—both in understanding fundamental principles and in applying them to practical affairs. May they strive earnestly in this! I respectfully write this postface at the end of the record.

Respectfully written by Qian Xili 錢習禮, Gentleman for Attendance and Academician Reader-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy at the Auxiliary Capital.
